
=================================================================
#37 Haemosu  (-37)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: Part II — The Dawn of War / The Seventh Invasion · place: buyeo_north · tone: founder fairy tale
Logline: Every day the sun crosses the sky on the same road. Today he looks down.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Every day the sun crosses the sky on the same road. Today he looks down.
[1] ¶ The sky is empty first. Then come five dragons in the yoke, gold, crimson, azure, jade and white, and behind them a small gold chariot cutting the noon on the run they make every day. From the ground it is a fleck and a wheel, nothing a bather could call a face. The driver stands in it the way a man stands in a doorway he owns, one palm on the rail, laughing at nothing in particular.
[2] [MAP -37: ]
[3] ¶ Dawn, noon, dusk, night, always the same route. Below, the Amnok is a line he is not supposed to break: wet stone, morning shallows with no boat in them, rocks that are only rocks.
[4] [PLACE amnok: Every god’s road crosses it. Most of them keep going.]
[5] ¶ **Haemosu**, god of the sun, has kept this hour since before the river had daughters. Today the Amnok flashes under the wheel. He looks down, and the hour breaks.
[6] [CARD Haemosu: The sun god. Punctual since before the rivers, until this afternoon.]
[7] ¶ In the shallows, three river-daughters are bathing: Yuhwa and her two sisters. Wet hair down their backs, the river at their hips. Nobody dressed for heaven. He falls in love and in lust in the same glance.
[8] [CARD Lady Yuhwa: The river’s youngest daughter, a nymph of the Amnok. Heaven is about to ruin her afternoon, or make it.]
[9] [CARD Hwahye: The eldest river-daughter. First into the water, every time.]
[10] [CARD Wihye: The middle sister. She laughs first and dives second.]
[11] ¶ Hwahye and Wihye have left their silk on the rocks. The eldest folded hers once; the middle did not bother. Yuhwa’s ice-blue is still on her shoulder, wet.
[12] ¶ Yuhwa kneels in the shallows with her hair in one fist like a dark rope and rinses the river out of it without hurrying. Heaven can wait on a rinse; she has decided that without saying it. With her back to the sky she looks over her shoulder, as if someone up there had said her name.
[13] Haemosu: …Stop. Stop the chariot.
[14] Haemosu: Those thighs… / The water…
[15] Lady Yuhwa: Unni. / Go. I’m here. / …I was going to say don’t look up.
[16] Hwahye: Hey. In. / Now. You hear me?
[17] ¶ Hwahye dives first and does not look back. The eldest treats the sky like a timetable she will not miss.
[18] Wihye: Pfft— wait up. / You, seriously— / Whatever, I’m going—
[19] ¶ Wihye laughs and follows, a splash that is mostly amusement.
[20] ¶ Two wakes cut the shallows and close. Yuhwa stays. She gets up off her knees, looks straight up as if she had been waiting for heaven to notice, and draws her wet hair over one shoulder.
[21] ¶ She draws the wet silk higher, one hip and then the other, and lets the sun finish looking.
[22] Haemosu: Hey— / Wait. Hey. You. / Why aren’t you hiding? Look at me like that and I’m coming down.
[23] Lady Yuhwa: Heaven looks down every day. / So today I’m supposed to blush? / …Come closer, if you want to see. / Into the water. / And decide… where your hands are going.
[24] Haemosu: …Your name. / I need it… before I come down. / Or… I kiss you without one.
[25] Lady Yuhwa: Come down first. / From the sky it’s an order. / At the water… I’ll hear it as a request. / Ask with your mouth… and I’ll answer with my name.
[26] ¶ He forgets how to swallow, a god doing a mortal’s small panic. Then he grins, and the grin arrives before the plan. He leaves the rail and the hour in the same motion, the dragons keep the joke going without him, and the water takes him at the knee.
[27] ¶ He wades close. She does not run. He stops where a stranger should stop. Then he doesn’t.
[28] Haemosu: Why didn’t you run away? / Your sisters did.
[29] Lady Yuhwa: …Didn’t see any reason. / The water’s cold. You’re warm. That’s all there is to it.
[30] Haemosu: Look straight at the sun / and you burn.
[31] Lady Yuhwa: Oh, is that so? / Then I should blink.
[32] Haemosu: It’ll burn your eyes out. / I’m not a lamp.
[33] Lady Yuhwa: I like what I see. / I’m looking anyway. You came down. / Don’t make me say it twice.
[34] ¶ He swallows. The grin survives it. Barely.
[35] ¶ She tips her mouth and asks whether the sun likes what it sees, silk already losing the argument with the water.
[36] Lady Yuhwa: This way. The bank. / The sky has too many sisters.
[37] ¶ He follows like the hour had been her idea.
[38] ¶ The copper room rises on the bank like a kiln. He builds it the same afternoon, because the open sky has become too many witnesses.
[39] Lady Yuhwa: Copper gets hot in summer. / …You’ll know if you touch it. / My back, too. / If you press me to it… you won’t tell which burned you.
[40] Haemosu: I know. / That’s why I can’t take my hands off you. / Or my mouth.
[41] Lady Yuhwa: Then don’t. / Not while heaven is watching.
[42] Lady Yuhwa: And while it watches… deeper.
[43] ¶ She kisses him with river still on her mouth. The kiss tastes like the shallows. He makes a sound he will deny.
[44] ¶ Inside, the copper has kept the afternoon’s heat. She leans into it and does not look away from him. Gold lies across wet skin in a hard bar, and the ice-blue silk slips from one shoulder, then gives up the other.
[45] Lady Yuhwa: If you want it, say so. / I’m not asking twice.
[46] Lady Yuhwa: Give me— all of it. / Don’t save any.
[47] ¶ He puts her back to it anyway. The river-silk is gathered at her hip and her thighs close around a sun-god who has never learned to be gentle with an hour. She takes him in with the same wet hand that washed her hair for heaven, and when he is all the way inside her she laughs, as if this were what she had meant by looking.
[48] Lady Yuhwa: Haa— is heaven always this heavy? / More— against the copper— don’t stop—
[49] Haemosu: I broke the hour. / I don’t care. / Your name— now—
[50] Lady Yuhwa: Yuhwa— ah— it’s Yuhwa— / Stay— stay inside me— / All of it— the whole sun—
[51] ¶ He takes her through the heat of the wall, gold on wet skin, and every stroke knocks a sound out of her that the river throws back. She comes first and loudly, looking up as if heaven were still watching. Then he spills into her, a god’s whole careless heat, and does not draw back, because she told him not to, and because the hour is already ruined.
[52] ¶ The copper keeps the afternoon. Outside, the river goes on being a river.
[53] ¶ Up on the road, the dragons have hauled an empty chariot to dusk on their own. Half the world got its evening late. Heaven noticed.
[54] Haemosu: They’re calling. / I’m late. I’m never late.
[55] Lady Yuhwa: Go, then. / …Come back tomorrow. Same hour. I’ll break it for you this time.
[56] Haemosu: They won’t let me come down twice. Not while I’m up there. / Hey. Don’t look at me like that. I’ll find a way.
[57] ¶ He goes up in a flash of copper. Heaven fines the sun the only way it can: while he is in the sky, he may not set foot on the earth. He may look. He may talk. That is all.
[58] ── SCENE: Habek's Court ──
[59] ¶ The copper is still warm when the river notices. The Amnok keeps its own court: **Habek**, god of the river and father of three daughters, stands on the wet stones as if the current were a hall. Mist is the dais. He does not need a chair.
[60] [CARD Habek: The Amnok’s river god. He keeps his borders the way kings do, and his daughters the same way.]
[61] Habek: Who stopped the chariot. Say a name.
[62] Lady Yuhwa: I… looked up. / I just— looked. That’s all it was.
[63] Habek: You don’t sleep in my mist after that. / You smell like copper.
[64] Habek: Go. The bank is closed.
[65] ¶ Hwahye and Wihye do not argue the sentence. The eldest watches the current. The middle one watches the copper glow die. Neither looks at their father’s face.
[66] ¶ Habek kicks Yuhwa out with a look, not a foot. The bank understands.
[67] ¶ The pavilion walkway does not catch her. Habek’s sleeve is already the closed door. She hits packed earth with ice-blue still wet from the copper.
[68] ¶ For a while nobody comes. The mist that used to be a bed is just weather. She sits where the river can see her and does not look up.
[69] ¶ The sky talks first. She hears him before she sees anything with paws.
[70] Haemosu: Hey. / Wait. Don’t sit in the dust. / Follow the fox.
[71] ¶ The fox is already on the packed earth, pale gold-white, looking back once as if she might miss the joke. Yuhwa follows it south, barefoot, the ice-blue gone dull with dust: pine shade, a river-bend that is not the Amnok, a pass of bare stone where she is smaller than the ridge. The fox does not explain the map.
[72] ── SCENE: Buyeo ──
[73] ¶ From the river, Buyeo’s capital is a palisade of timber teeth and a hill of grey roofs. The studded doors open. King Geumwa, the gold-frog king, comes out to the yard himself.
[74] [CARD King Geumwa: The gold-frog king. Found under a rock, raised in a palace, kind to strays.]
[75] [PLACE buyeo_north: An old kingdom that takes in strays and keeps count.]
[76] King Geumwa: Come in. I’ve got a room free. / The yard can learn your name later.
[77] ¶ A sun-shaft finds her where she kneels to wring the river out of her sleeve. When she crosses the yard at night it moves with her, a bar of gold keeping her sleeve.
[78] ¶ Yuhwa’s ice-blue sleeve is the first roof the boy will remember, though he is not a boy yet.
[79] ¶ In time Yuhwa lays a great egg. Geumwa has the egg taken from her before the court has agreed what a river-daughter is allowed to bear.
[80] ¶ **Dogs won't eat it. An axe won't split it. What on earth is inside Yuhwa's egg…?**
